title: Requests Get
description: Make HTTP GET requests using the requests library
code:
import requests

# Basic GET request:
response = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
print(response.status_code)  # 200
print(response.text)          # Raw response body
print(response.json())        # Parse as JSON (dict)
print(response.headers)       # Response headers

# Query parameters:
params = {"q": "python", "page": 1, "per_page": 10}
response = requests.get("https://api.github.com/search/repositories", params=params)
print(response.url)  # https://api.github.com/...?q=python&page=1&per_page=10

# Custom headers:
headers = {"User-Agent": "MyApp/1.0", "Authorization": "Bearer token123"}
response = requests.get("https://api.github.com/user", headers=headers)

# Timeout:
try:
    response = requests.get("https://example.com", timeout=5)
except requests.Timeout:
    print("Request timed out")

# Response validation:
response = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
response.raise_for_status()  # Raise HTTPError for 4xx/5xx

# Streaming:
response = requests.get("https://example.com/large-file", stream=True)
for chunk in response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
    process(chunk)

# Session for connection reuse:
with requests.Session() as session:
    session.headers.update({"Authorization": "Bearer token"})
    resp1 = session.get("https://api.github.com/user")
    resp2 = session.get("https://api.github.com/repos")

# Error handling:
try:
    response = requests.get("https://nonexistent.domain", timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()
except requests.ConnectionError:
    print("Could not connect")
except requests.Timeout:
    print("Timeout")
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    print(f"HTTP {e.response.status_code}: {e}")
except requests.RequestException as e:
    print(f"Request failed: {e}")
explanation: requests.get() fetches URLs. Use .json() to parse JSON, params for query strings, and timeout.

title: Requests Post
description: Send HTTP POST requests with data
code:
import requests

# POST with form data:
data = {"username": "alice", "password": "secret123"}
response = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", data=data)
print(response.json())

# POST with JSON:
json_data = {"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}
response = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", json=json_data)

# POST with files:
files = {"file": ("report.pdf", open("report.pdf", "rb"), "application/pdf")}
response = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files=files)

# POST with auth:
from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth
response = requests.post(
    "https://api.example.com/login",
    auth=HTTPBasicAuth("user", "pass"),
    json={"scope": "read"}
)

# PUT, DELETE, PATCH:
response = requests.put("https://api.example.com/users/1", json={"name": "Bob"})
response = requests.delete("https://api.example.com/users/1")
response = requests.patch("https://api.example.com/users/1", json={"age": 31})

# Cookies:
response = requests.get("https://example.com", cookies={"session": "abc123"})
print(response.cookies)  # RequestsCookieJar

# Redirect handling:
response = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/redirect/3", allow_redirects=True)
print(response.history)  # List of redirect responses
print(response.url)      # Final URL after redirects

# Download file:
response = requests.get("https://example.com/image.jpg")
with open("image.jpg", "wb") as f:
    f.write(response.content)

# Upload file with progress:
with open("data.csv", "rb") as f:
    response = requests.post("https://httpbin.org/post", files={"file": f})
explanation: requests.post() with data= for forms, json= for JSON, files= for uploads. Use Session for connection reuse.

title: Unittest Basics
description: Write and run unit tests using unittest
code:
import unittest

# Function to test:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero")
    return a / b

class TestMathOperations(unittest.TestCase):
    
    def setUp(self):
        """Runs before each test method."""
        self.values = [(1, 2), (5, 3), (10, -2)]
    
    def tearDown(self):
        """Runs after each test method."""
        pass
    
    def test_add(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(2, 3), 5)
        self.assertEqual(add(-1, 1), 0)
        self.assertEqual(add(0, 0), 0)
    
    def test_add_float(self):
        self.assertAlmostEqual(add(0.1, 0.2), 0.3)
    
    def test_divide(self):
        self.assertEqual(divide(10, 2), 5)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(divide(1, 3), 0.33333333, places=5)
    
    def test_divide_by_zero(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            divide(10, 0)
    
    def test_with_values(self):
        for a, b in self.values:
            result = add(a, b)
            self.assertEqual(result, a + b)
    
    def test_type_error(self):
        with self.assertRaises(TypeError):
            add("hello", 5)

# Run tests:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

# Common assertions:
# assertEqual(a, b)          — a == b
# assertNotEqual(a, b)       — a != b
# assertTrue(x)              — bool(x) is True
# assertFalse(x)             — bool(x) is False
# assertIs(a, b)             — a is b
# assertIsNone(x)            — x is None
# assertIn(a, b)             — a in b
# assertIsInstance(a, b)     — isinstance(a, b)
# assertAlmostEqual(a, b)    — round(a-b, 7) == 0
# assertRaises(Exception)    — raises exception
# assertGreater(a, b)        — a > b
# assertLess(a, b)           — a < b
explanation: unittest.TestCase provides test methods with setUp/tearDown. Use assertEqual, assertRaises, etc.

title: Unittest Mock
description: Mock objects for testing external dependencies
code:
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch, MagicMock
import unittest

# Basic Mock:
mock = Mock()
mock.return_value = 42
print(mock())  # 42

# Verify calls:
mock(1, 2, key="value")
mock.assert_called_once()
mock.assert_called_with(1, 2, key="value")
print(mock.call_count)  # 1

# Side effects:
mock = Mock()
mock.side_effect = [10, 20, 30]  # Returns different each call
print(mock())  # 10
print(mock())  # 20
print(mock())  # 30

# Side effect with exception:
mock.side_effect = ValueError("error")
try:
    mock()
except ValueError:
    print("Caught!")

# MagicMock (supports magic methods):
mm = MagicMock()
mm.__len__.return_value = 5
print(len(mm))  # 5

# @patch decorator:
class APIClient:
    def fetch_data(self):
        import requests
        response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data")
        return response.json()

class TestAPIClient(unittest.TestCase):
    @patch("requests.get")
    def test_fetch_data(self, mock_get):
        # Configure mock
        mock_response = Mock()
        mock_response.json.return_value = {"key": "value"}
        mock_get.return_value = mock_response
        
        # Test
        client = APIClient()
        result = client.fetch_data()
        
        self.assertEqual(result, {"key": "value"})
        mock_get.assert_called_once_with("https://api.example.com/data")

# Patch as context manager:
def get_user(user_id):
    import requests
    resp = requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")
    return resp.json()

with patch("requests.get") as mock_get:
    mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"id": 1, "name": "Alice"}
    user = get_user(1)
    print(user["name"])  # Alice

# Mock with spec:
from unittest.mock import create_autospec

def compute(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2

mocked_func = create_autospec(compute, return_value=10)
print(mocked_func(5))  # 10
# mocked_func("hello", "world")  # TypeError: too many args
explanation: Mock objects simulate real dependencies. patch() replaces objects during tests. MagicMock supports dunder methods.

title: Pip Command Basics
code:
# Install packages:
# pip install requests
# pip install flask==2.3.0         Specific version
# pip install requests>=2.28,<3   Version range
# pip install numpy pandas          Multiple packages
# pip install -r requirements.txt  From file

# List installed:
# pip list                    # All packages
# pip list --outdated         # Outdated packages

# Show package info:
# pip show requests           # Version, location, dependencies

# Uninstall:
# pip uninstall requests
# pip uninstall -y requests   # Skip confirmation

# Freeze (create requirements):
# pip freeze > requirements.txt

# Upgrade:
# pip install --upgrade pip
# pip install --upgrade requests

# Install in development mode:
# pip install -e .           # Install package from current dir

# Search (pip >= 21.2 removed search, use pip index):
# pip index versions requests

# Check dependencies:
# pip check                  # Verify installed packages

# Download without installing:
# pip download requests -d ./packages

# requirements.txt format:
# requests>=2.28,<3
# flask==2.3.0
# numpy>=1.24
# pytest>=7.0
# # Comments are allowed

# Lock file (pip freeze > requirements.txt):
"""
Package==Version Info
```
# Example:
requests==2.31.0
flask==2.3.2
numpy==1.24.3
pandas==2.0.1
```
"""
explanation: pip installs packages. Use pip freeze > requirements.txt to lock versions. Use venv for isolation.

title: Virtual Environments (venv)
description: Create isolated Python environments using venv
code:
# Create virtual environment:
# python -m venv venv
# python -m venv /path/to/env

# On Windows:
# venv\Scripts\activate

# On macOS/Linux:
# source venv/bin/activate

# Deactivate:
# deactivate

# After activation, pip installs go to the venv:
# pip install requests  # Installed only in this venv

# Delete venv and recreate:
# rm -rf venv          # Unix
# rmdir /s venv        # Windows
# python -m venv venv  # Recreate

# Using venv in Python script:
import subprocess
import sys

def create_and_install(env_path: str, packages: list[str]):
    """Create venv and install packages."""
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "venv", env_path], check=True)
    
    # Determine pip path:
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        pip_path = f"{env_path}/Scripts/pip"
    else:
        pip_path = f"{env_path}/bin/pip"
    
    # Install packages:
    subprocess.run([pip_path, "install", *packages], check=True)

# Requirements file in venv:
# (venv) $ pip install -r requirements.txt
# (venv) $ pip list  # Only packages for this project

# Freeze venv packages:
# (venv) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt
explanation: venv creates isolated Python environments. Always use venv per project. pip installs go inside the venv.

title: Numpy Array Creation
description: Create NumPy arrays from lists or using built-in functions
code:
import numpy as np

# From list:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(a)        # [1 2 3 4 5]
print(a.shape)  # (5,)
print(a.dtype)  # int64

# 2D array:
b = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(b.shape)  # (2, 3)
print(b[0, 1])  # 2

# Zeros and ones:
zeros = np.zeros((3, 4))        # 3x4 zeros
ones = np.ones((2, 3))           # 2x3 ones
identity = np.eye(4)             # 4x4 identity

# Range:
r1 = np.arange(10)               # [0, 1, ..., 9]
r2 = np.arange(2, 10, 2)         # [2, 4, 6, 8]
r3 = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)        # [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]

# Random:
rand = np.random.rand(3, 3)      # Uniform [0,1)
randn = np.random.randn(100)     # Normal distribution
randint = np.random.randint(0, 10, size=5)  # Random ints

# Reshape:
a = np.arange(12)
print(a.reshape(3, 4))
print(a.reshape(2, 2, 3))        # 3D array

# Data types:
print(np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32))
print(np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.complex128))

# Copy vs view:
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
view = arr[1:3]                  # View (shares data)
copy = arr[[1, 2]]               # Copy (independent)

# Constants:
print(np.pi)      # 3.14159...
print(np.inf)     # inf
print(np.nan)     # nan
explanation: NumPy provides n-dimensional arrays. Key functions: array(), zeros(), arange(), linspace(), reshape().

title: Numpy Operations
code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
b = np.array([5, 6, 7, 8])

# Vectorized operations (element-wise):
print(a + b)      # [6, 8, 10, 12]
print(a * b)      # [5, 12, 21, 32]
print(a ** 2)     # [1, 4, 9, 16]
print(np.sqrt(a)) # [1, 1.414, 1.732, 2]

# Broadcasting:
print(a + 10)     # [11, 12, 13, 14]
print(a * 2)      # [2, 4, 6, 8]

# Universal functions:
print(np.sin(a))  # Trig functions
print(np.exp(a))  # Exponential
print(np.log(a))  # Natural log

# Aggregation:
print(np.sum(a))      # 10
print(np.mean(a))     # 2.5
print(np.std(a))      # 1.118...
print(np.min(a))      # 1
print(np.max(a))      # 4
print(np.argmax(a))   # 3 (index of max)
print(np.median(a))   # 2.5

# 2D aggregation:
matrix = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.sum(matrix, axis=0))  # [4, 6]  (column sum)
print(np.sum(matrix, axis=1))  # [3, 7]  (row sum)

# Masking/Boolean indexing:
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
mask = arr > 3
print(mask)                # [False, False, False, True, True]
print(arr[mask])           # [4, 5]
print(arr[arr % 2 == 0])   # [2, 4] (even numbers)

# Linear algebra:
x = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
y = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(np.dot(x, y))        # Matrix multiplication
print(x @ y)               # Same (Python 3.5+)
print(np.linalg.inv(x))    # Matrix inverse

# Sorting:
arr = np.array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
print(np.sort(arr))        # [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]
print(np.argsort(arr))     # [1, 3, 0, 2, 4] (indices)
explanation: NumPy operations are vectorized (fast, no Python loops). Broadcasting applies scalars to arrays.

title: Pandas Series
description: Create and manipulate pandas Series (1D labeled array)
code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Create Series:
s = pd.Series([1, 3, 5, np.nan, 6, 8])
print(s)
print(s.values)  # array([1, 3, 5, nan, 6, 8])
print(s.index)   # RangeIndex(start=0, stop=6, step=1)

# With custom index:
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["a", "b", "c"])
print(s["b"])    # 20

# From dict:
data = {"Alice": 30, "Bob": 25, "Charlie": 35}
s = pd.Series(data)
print(s["Alice"])  # 30

# Operations:
print(s + 10)       # Add 10 to all
print(s.mean())     # 30.0
print(s.median())   # 30.0
print(s.describe())  # Count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max

# Filtering:
print(s[s > 30])   # Values > 30

# Apply function:
print(s.apply(lambda x: x * 2))

# Handling missing:
print(s.isna())
print(s.fillna(0))
print(s.dropna())

# Vectorized string:
s = pd.Series(["hello", "world", "python"])
print(s.str.upper())
print(s.str.len())

# Index-based operations:
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], index=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(s.loc[10:30])   # Label-based indexing
print(s.iloc[0:3])    # Position-based indexing

# Statistical:
print(s.sum())        # 15
print(s.std())        # 1.58...
print(s.min())        # 1
print(s.max())        # 5
print(s.idxmax())     # Index of max: 50
print(s.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]))
explanation: Series is a 1D labeled array. Access by label (loc) or position (iloc). Supports vectorized operations.

title: Pandas DataFrame
description: Create and manipulate pandas DataFrames (2D labeled data)
code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# From dict:
data = {
    "Name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 35, 28],
    "City": ["NYC", "Boston", "Chicago", "Denver"],
    "Salary": [70000, 85000, 65000, 90000]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

# From CSV:
# df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
# df = pd.read_csv("data.csv", index_col=0)
# df = pd.read_csv("data.csv", parse_dates=["Date"])

# Basic info:
print(df.head(2))      # First 2 rows
print(df.tail())        # Last 5 rows
print(df.info())        # Column types, non-null counts
print(df.describe())    # Statistical summary
print(df.shape)         # (4, 4) rows, columns
print(df.columns)       # Column names
print(df.dtypes)        # Column types

# Column access:
print(df["Name"])      # Series
print(df[["Name", "Age"]])  # DataFrame
print(df.Name)          # Attribute access (if valid name)

# Row access:
print(df.loc[0])        # First row (by label)
print(df.iloc[0])       # First row (by position)
print(df.loc[0:2])      # Rows 0, 1, 2

# Filtering:
print(df[df["Age"] > 28])
print(df[(df["Age"] > 25) & (df["City"] == "NYC")])

# Add column:
df["Bonus"] = df["Salary"] * 0.1
df["Total"] = df["Salary"] + df["Bonus"]

# Drop column:
df = df.drop("Bonus", axis=1)

# Group by:
print(df.groupby("City").mean())
print(df.groupby("City")["Salary"].agg(["mean", "sum", "count"]))

# Sort:
print(df.sort_values("Salary", ascending=False))

# Apply:
df["Name_Upper"] = df["Name"].apply(lambda x: x.upper())

# Save:
# df.to_csv("output.csv", index=False)
# df.to_excel("output.xlsx", index=False)

# Check for missing:
print(df.isnull().sum())

# Fill missing:
# df["column"] = df["column"].fillna(df["column"].mean())

# Unique values:
print(df["City"].unique())
print(df["City"].value_counts())
explanation: DataFrame is a 2D labeled data structure. Read from CSV with read_csv(). Use loc/iloc for row access.

title: Pandas Groupby Aggregation
description: Group, aggregate, and pivot data in pandas
code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Department": ["IT", "HR", "IT", "HR", "IT", "Finance"],
    "Employee": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Eve", "Frank"],
    "Salary": [70000, 50000, 80000, 55000, 90000, 60000],
    "Years": [5, 3, 8, 2, 10, 4]
})

# Basic groupby:
print(df.groupby("Department")["Salary"].mean())
print(df.groupby("Department")["Salary"].agg(["mean", "sum", "count", "std"]))

# Multiple aggregations:
print(df.groupby("Department").agg({
    "Salary": ["mean", "max", "min"],
    "Years": "mean"
}))

# Group by multiple columns:
print(df.groupby(["Department", "Years"]).size())

# Pivot table:
pivot = df.pivot_table(
    values="Salary",
    index="Department",
    columns="Years",
    aggfunc="mean",
    fill_value=0
)
print(pivot)

# Merge (SQL-style join):
employees = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "dept_id": [1, 2, 1]
})
departments = pd.DataFrame({
    "dept_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "dept_name": ["Engineering", "HR", "Finance"]
})

merged = pd.merge(employees, departments, on="dept_id", how="left")
print(merged)

# Concat:
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2], "B": [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"A": [5, 6], "B": [7, 8]})
result = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)
print(result)

# Apply with groupby:
def top_salary(grp):
    return grp.nlargest(2, "Salary")

print(df.groupby("Department").apply(top_salary))

# Value counts:
print(df["Department"].value_counts(normalize=True))  # Percentages
explanation: groupby() splits data into groups. agg() applies functions. merge() joins DataFrames. pivot_table() summaries.
